svg.text: DataPilot AI — how it works, tab by tab
Upload, automatic analysis, then what you do by hand versus what the AI does — for every tab up to Governance.
the AI model is called for this step
fixed code decides — same answer every time, no tokens
Drag and drop, any of the formats below
· max 50 MB · rejected if empty or the extension isn't allowed
No AI here — this is all fixed code
The extension must be allowed, the size must be under 50 MB and the file must not be empty. Anything else is refused before a single row is read.
Work out the format, then read it
The encoding is detected from the first 100 KB. For a CSV the real separator is found by testing comma, semicolon, pipe, tab and tilde. Excel, JSON and Parquet use their own reader.
Spaces are trimmed and repeated names are made unique, so the table can be stored safely.
The same upload is then written to three places, each with a different job:
An exact copy, kept only as proof of what you sent. Never changed, never read again.
A fast columnar version. Everything from here on reads and rewrites this file.
Format, encoding, separator, row and column counts. Facts about the file — never the rows themselves.
Analysis then starts on its own — you don't have to press anything.
the working copy is the input from here on
No clicks needed. This also re-runs after every fix, edit or new rule
Three AI agents run in order, one after another

They share a single working memory: each agent reads what the one before it worked out and adds its own findings. If an agent fails, only that agent's part is missing — the rest still completes. This is where the score, the issue list and the sensitivity classification come from.
Understands the shape of your data
Load the stored table into memory.
Work out each column's basic type
Work out what each column means
14 business types are recognised — email, phone, postcode, web address,
latitude/longitude, money, date, ID, category — from the shape of the values plus the
How much is missing, how many different values, smallest, largest, average, and a few real
result → what every column is and contains
Finds the problems and scores them
Over 20 independent checks look for missing values, blanks, duplicate rows and columns,
columns that never change, too many or too few distinct values, badly formed emails,
phones, web addresses and dates, unexpected negatives, stray spaces, inconsistent
Which column, how serious, how many rows, and which of the six quality areas it damages.
Score each of the six areas
Every area starts at 100 and loses points based on how serious the problem is and how much
Integrity 10% — giving the headline number out of 100.
result → the issue list and the 0-100 score
Judges sensitivity — the only AI call here
Column names and detected meanings are matched against personal, financial and health
Fixed rules make this call, so it is identical on every run and can be defended in an
audit. The AI is not allowed to change it.
Ask the AI to write the human layer
The AI supplies business-friendly column names, one-line descriptions and the wording that
explains the classification. Columns go in batches of 20 to keep the cost down.
Carry on without it if needed
If the AI is unavailable or returns something unusable, the rule-based result is kept
Only one step in this whole stage calls the model

Agent 3 asks the AI to write the descriptions and the explanation text. Everything else — the types, the checks and the score — is fixed code, on purpose: the same file must always produce the same score, it has to stand up to an audit, and re-analysis runs after every fix and edit so it needs to
Your own saved rules are run and added to the issue list
Issues you chose to ignore are removed
Everything is saved so the tabs can just read it

Score 75 or above and it is cleared automatically. Below 75 and it is marked as needing review — the app shows a banner with Approve and Reject, and until someone chooses, the dataset is not treated as fit to use.
now you open the dataset and work through the tabs
You read what the dataset actually contains before touching anything
Read the row and column counts, the format, encoding and separator that
Scan the column list with each column's detected meaning and how much
Page through the real rows, 50 at a time.
Decide whether this is even the right file before doing any work on it.
None of this recalculates anything — it is all read back from Stage 2, so the
Writes a plain-English summary of the dataset
The story is requested once, in the background.
The AI is given a summary, not your rows
It receives the column names, their detected meanings, the row count and the quality score. The actual data values are not sent, so nothing sensitive leaves the app.
A few sentences on what this dataset appears to be about, what the important columns mean, and what stands out as unusual.
It is saved for next time
The story is stored on the dataset, so it is written once. Every later visit is instant and costs nothing. You can force a rewrite if the data has changed a lot.
You still get a summary — assembled from the numbers instead of written as prose.
you get → a short readable description of the dataset
You see the score and the problems, then either write your own rule or let the AI fix an issue
Read the overall score and the six area bars.
Filter the issue list by status or severity.
Open an issue to see the affected rows.
Mark an issue as ignored if it is acceptable for your use — it stops
counting against the score and can be brought back at any time.
Every issue already comes with a written explanation produced by fixed code,
which is why this page never waits for the AI.
Turns a finding into something you can act on
You ask for more detail on an issue
The built-in explanation is shown immediately; the AI version is only fetched if you want it.
The AI is given the finding, not the data
It sees the check name, the column, the severity and how many rows are affected — never the row values.
What is wrong, why it usually happens, what it costs you in practice, and what to do about it.
Falls back to the standard wording for that check, so there is never a blank explanation.
Your own rule, written in English
You describe the rule — the AI only translates it
For example "salary should never be negative" or "order date cannot be in the future".
The AI turns it into a real condition
It converts your sentence into something the app can actually run against the data. Nothing has run yet.
The condition is run against the working copy and reports how many rows break the rule, with up to 10 real examples.
If it doesn't work, it is repaired
Type mismatches are corrected automatically and retried. If it still fails, the AI gets exactly one attempt to fix it.
You see the result before anything is saved
It shows "this flags N of M rows" with the examples, so you can judge whether the rule is right.
You approve it — or it is discarded
Only on approval is the rule stored, and from then on it runs inside every future analysis. Reject and nothing is kept.
you get → a permanent check of your own, in your words
The AI decides nothing here — the change is a fixed rule
You click Fix on an issue
Or Fix all, which does every fixable issue as one batch.
If the issue has no proven fix, the request is refused and you are pointed at cleaning instead.
An undo point is created first
Before anything changes, so it can always be put back.
The change follows a fixed rule
Missing numbers become the middle value, missing text becomes the most common value, stray spaces
are trimmed, duplicate rows are dropped. The AI is not asked what to change.
The before and after value of each one, so the edit is fully traceable.
The whole of Stage 2 runs again, so you immediately see the new score and what is left.
You can undo any of it
One fix, a whole batch, or everything.
you get → a corrected dataset, a new score, and a full audit trail
Filter down to the rows you care about.
Click a cell and type the correct value.
Undo the last edit if you got it wrong.
Edits are treated exactly like a fix: snapshotted first, recorded cell by cell,
The app does not guess what you meant or propose replacement values. What you type is what is stored.
An undo point is taken before the edit, every changed cell is recorded with its old and new value, and the score is recalculated afterwards — the same safety net the fix agent gets.
A manual edit is a statement of fact about your business that only you can make. Letting a model influence it would quietly put guesses into data you believe you verified by hand.
You get a dashboard without building one, then ask for extra widgets in words
Read the KPIs and charts that were chosen for you.
Tick which ones you want to keep — your selection is saved.
Accept or reject any widget the AI proposes.
Ask a widget to explain itself.
The starting dashboard involves no AI at all — it is built from what Stage 2
already worked out about your columns.
Chosen by rules, from the column types
Using each column's detected meaning, the app lists every KPI and chart the data could genuinely support.
A sensible default set is picked
So the tab is useful the moment you open it, with no prompting and no waiting.
A total needs a number, a trend needs a date, a breakdown needs a category. Impossible combinations are never offered.
Asking for a widget in words
You describe it — the AI plans it, you confirm it
For example "average revenue by state" or "spend vs units".
Your column names are checked first
If nothing in your request matches a real column, it stops and says so rather than charting
something unrelated. This is the guard that stops confident nonsense.
If you named the chart type, you win
Saying "spend vs units" means a scatter plot, and your wording overrides the AI's guess.
It chooses which columns to use, which chart type and whether to total or average.
The plan is checked against reality
A chart the columns cannot support is thrown away and a simpler keyword method tries instead. If
that also fails you get a clear refusal, not a broken chart.
If it matched a misspelt column to a real one, it tells you which substitution it made.
It is proposed, never silently added
You see the finished widget and choose whether to keep it.
you get → a widget you asked for in plain words, with the reasoning shown
You ask questions about the data in plain English
Type a question the way you would ask a colleague.
Read the answer, the table behind it and the chart.
Ask follow-ups — the conversation is remembered.
Clear the history when you want a clean start.
History is saved per dataset and restored when you come back, so follow-ups
Understand, query, then explain — with a fallback at every step
"How many rows" is answered by counting them. "Give me insights" goes straight to the summary
generator. No model needed, no chance of a vague reply.
It reads your question plus the last few turns of the conversation and decides whether this needs
a query over the data or just a reply — so "now show that as a pie chart" still makes sense.
If it came back with neither a query nor a real answer, or with a brush-off like "please run a
query yourself", it is thrown away here. You never see those.
A backup method takes over if needed
The app assembles a query itself from the columns your question mentions and any filter it
implies. This is what keeps Chat working when the AI is completely offline.
It can only read. Anything that would change or delete data is blocked, and a row limit is always
applied — even if the model asked for it.
If the planned query errors, the backup query runs instead so you still get an answer.
A chart is chosen for the result
Based on the shape of what came back, unless you asked for a specific type.
One or two sentences saying what the table actually shows, and the exchange is saved for your next
you get → a sentence, the table it came from, and a chart
You see how sensitive this dataset is and how it should be handled
Read the sensitivity classification and why it was given.
Review the list of columns holding personal data.
Read the recommended handling tier and the reasoning.
Check the business description of each column.
As a steward, approve or reject the dataset on this basis.
This is the tab an auditor would ask to see, which is why the AI has the
Rules make the decision — the AI only writes it up
Column names and detected meanings are matched against known personal, financial and health
patterns — names, contact details, identifiers, dates of birth, salary, account and card fields,
From what was found. Fixed rules, so the same dataset always produces the same answer and it can
Based on the sensitivity and the size of the dataset. Also fixed rules.
Only now is the AI involved
It is asked to write the business-friendly column names, the one-line descriptions and the
readable rationale. It cannot change the classification, the personal-data list or the tier —
Columns are sent in batches of 20
To stay inside the model's limits on wide tables, and to keep the cost predictable.
If the AI fails, nothing is lost
Unavailable, erroring or malformed output all lead to the same place: the rule-based result is
kept exactly as computed. The compliance answer never depends on the model being up.
you get → a defensible classification, plus readable descriptions on top
The AI never decides a number
Scores, classifications and fixes are computed by rules, so they are
Descriptions, explanations, stories and narration — the parts where language
Most AI calls see only column names, types and counts — not the values.
It all works with the AI off
Every AI step has a fixed-code fallback, so nothing becomes unusable.
